newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore cabinet moves only first stage -analyst.
newsitem.headline: Singapore cabinet moves only first stage -analyst.

text.p: Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's recently announced cabinet reshuffle may be a prelude to wider changes at key economic and international ministries within a year, political analysts said on Sunday.

"Twelve months down the line we might find Tony Tan (Defence) and Richard Hu (Finance) bowing out in favour of some of the new talent that has been brought in," predicted Bruce Gale of the Political and Economic Risk Consultancy.
Gale told Reuters newly-elected members of parliament like former Shell chief executive Peter Chen would be front-runners to take senior positions in short order.
"New back-benchers can get into a ministry very quickly after joining the government," he said, tipping Chen for a senior economic brief in the next 12 to 24 months.

Gale said others likely to benefit from further changes could be new Education Minister Teo Chee Hean, who he said was "on the way up" and Minister of State for Defence Matthias Yao who "plainly has the Prime Minister's eye".
Teo's appointment as education minister was one of four posts changed in the reshuffle and one of the two most important briefs awarded alongside trade and industry, analysts said.
The high profile trade ministry, seen to carry increasing international clout as Singapore positions itself as a global business hub, was given to Lee Yock Suan.
Gale said trade was a brief observers had been "watching closely in recent months because of the recent performance of the economy".

Another cabinet minister involved in the reshuffle was George Yeo, who remained Minister of Information and the Arts but relinquished his Health portfolio while becoming Second Minister at Trade and Industry.
Yeo Cheow Tong left trade and industry to claim back the health minister's job he left in 1994. He was also given the environment brief.

The possibility of more cabinet changes was raised when Saturday's reshuffle was announced. Goh's office said they would come within two years, during which time the incumbent ministers for communications and national development would see through the implementation of major programmes.
No details of the likely changes were given.
Saturday's reshuffle followed a landslide general election victory earlier this month in which the ruling People's Action Party was returned to power with 81 of 83 parliamentary seats.
The changes met with mixed reaction from commentators who expressed surprise no new blood had been brought in at cabinet level.

A European diplomat in Singapore told Reuters he was "quite surprised there are not more changes, especially as Goh has said he wanted to bring in the people who would lead the country into the next century".
